Content covers: the closing parable of the naphtha and balsam seller illustrating that sustenance belongs to God alone; the teaching that sin dulls the heart, drawing on the deliberate misreading of 'venitmeitem' as 'venitamtem'; the mirror-principle teaching that both impurity and holiness compound from small beginnings to large, from below to above, and from this world to the next; the chapter-heading transition into the new mishnah on the lottery of the two goats, including the urn's own construction from wood (rather than consecrated material, so as not to require metal or the Temple treasury's own funds) and the procedure of drawing and placing the lots; the extended discussion of why the Torah is considerate of property, working from earthenware purification laws up through an a fortiori argument to the property of the righteous; the deputy high priest's own role when the lot for the Name comes up in his own hand rather than the high priest's; Rabbi Chanina's own explanation for why the deputy always stands at the high priest's right; the mishnah's own extended baraita on the forty years of Shimon HaTzaddik's own service, during which the lot for the Name always rose in the right hand, the crimson strap always turned white (a sign of divine forgiveness, tied to Rashi's own extensive digression on identifying the 'western lamp' via Shabbat 22b, Menachot 98b, Mishnah Tamid 6:1, and Numbers 8), and the fire of the arrangement always burned strong; and the closing account of the reversal of these signs after Shimon HaTzaddik's own death, including the diminished showbread portions and the modest priests' own restraint from taking a doubled share, closing into the daf-boundary comment that continues onto 39b.
